explanation: Rémi is the central character of Hector Malot's novel Sans Famille — the story follows his life journey as an orphan boy. Vitalis is the travelling musician who takes Rémi under his guardianship, while Mère Barberin is his foster mother who raises him in the village. Joli-Cœur is simply Vitalis's pet monkey, not a human character. The entire plot revolves around Rémi's quest to discover his true identity and family.

A literary genre written entirely in the form of dialogue between characters is called une pièce (a play or theatrical piece). Un conte is a short tale or story narrated by a storyteller, and un roman is a long prose novel told through narration. Un poème is written in verse form with rhythm and imagery. Only a play (pièce de théâtre) uses dialogue as its primary structural form, meant to be performed on stage.

In Sans Famille, Mr. and Mrs. Driscoll are portrayed as aristocrats — wealthy English nobles living in a grand estate. This is significant because Rémi's true origins are connected to this upper-class English family. The Driscoll household represents privilege and wealth, contrasting with Rémi's poor upbringing in France. They are not mariners, thieves, or ordinary people, but members of the English upper class.

Dr. Mariama speaks the line 'Enfermer la femme, ça ne sert à rien' in Chaque chose en son temps, expressing a progressive view on women's freedom. Dr. Mariama is a modern, educated female character whose views contrast with more traditional male characters in the story. El-Hadji and Fatou have different roles and do not deliver this particular feminist statement. This line is one of the key quotes that reveals the novel's themes around gender and tradition.

Chaque chose en son temps was written by Lynn Mbuko, a Nigerian author writing in French. Camara Laye is famous for L'Enfant Noir, a classic Guinean novel, not this work. Margaret Kwakwa and Tunde Ajiboye are not associated with this text. Lynn Mbuko's work is part of the Nigerian Francophone literary tradition taught in Nigerian schools and examined by JAMB.

The CFA franc (Franc de la Communauté Financière d'Afrique) is the single currency used across French-speaking West African countries like Sénégal, Côte d'Ivoire, and Mali. The livre (pound) is the currency of Britain, while the cedi belongs to Ghana, an English-speaking country. The FF (Franc Français) was France's own currency before it adopted the Euro in 2002. The CFA remains the standard monetary unit in the West African francophone zone.

The CFTD (Centre de Formation des Techniciens du Développement), a French-language technical training institution in Nigeria, is located in Jos, Plateau State. Ilorin, Badagry, and Keffi are other Nigerian cities but do not host this particular French institution. Jos was chosen partly because of its central location in Nigeria. This is a factual geography question about French cultural and educational presence in Nigeria.

Nicolas Sarkozy succeeded Jacques Chirac as President of France, winning the 2007 presidential election. François Mitterrand served before Chirac from 1981 to 1995, and Valéry Giscard d'Estaing served before Mitterrand from 1974 to 1981. Jean-Marie Le Pen was Sarkozy's political rival but never became president — he lost to Chirac in the 2002 runoff. The correct chronological order is Giscard d'Estaing → Mitterrand → Chirac → Sarkozy.

Sénégal is both a Francophone country and located in West Africa, making it the correct answer. Ghana is in West Africa but is an English-speaking country. Kenya is in East Africa and is English/Swahili-speaking, so it fails both criteria. Gabon is Francophone but is situated in Central Africa, not West Africa. Only Sénégal satisfies both conditions — French-speaking and West African.

France's national holiday, known as La Fête Nationale or Bastille Day, is celebrated on July 14th every year, commemorating the storming of the Bastille prison in 1789, a key event of the French Revolution. July 4th is Independence Day in the United States, a common distractor in this question. July 2nd and July 20th have no significant connection to French national celebrations. Every French-speaking student should know that 'le quatorze juillet' is one of the most important dates in French history and culture.

The passage describes the author being most spoiled during his childhood years, making 'pendant son enfance' the correct answer. Childhood is when parents tend to indulge children the most, and the text supports this. 'Pendant les vacances' refers only to holidays, which is a limited period within childhood. Being spoiled 'à l'âge adulte' or 'à l'école' contradicts the tone and events described in the passage.

The passage describes the author being most spoiled during his childhood years, making 'pendant son enfance' the correct answer. Childhood is when parents tend to indulge children the most, and the text supports this. 'Pendant les vacances' refers only to holidays, which is a limited period within childhood. Being spoiled 'à l'âge adulte' or 'à l'école' contradicts the tone and events described in the passage.

The passage presents the father as generally 'avare' (stingy or miserly), meaning he was reluctant to spend money freely. This is a key character trait established in the text. 'Méchant' means wicked or mean, which goes beyond what the text says. 'Travailleur' means hardworking and 'triste' means sad — neither matches the father's dominant character description in the passage.

At the time of the story, the author's parents had only one child — the author himself — making option D correct. This detail from the passage explains why so much attention and indulgence was directed at him. Options A and B misrepresent the parents' character and financial status as described. Option C directly contradicts D, and the passage makes clear the author was an only child.

The text presents the author as an intelligent child, as shown by his ability to perform well and observe the world around him. Intelligence is explicitly or implicitly affirmed in the passage's description of his actions and thoughts. 'Frustré' (frustrated) and 'paresseux' (lazy) are contradicted by his engagement with life on the farm and at home. 'Idiot' is entirely unsupported by the text.

The noun 'robe' is feminine singular in French, so the interrogative adjective must agree with it — 'Quelle' is the correct feminine singular form. Interrogative adjectives in French must match the gender and number of the noun they qualify. 'Quel' is masculine singular and cannot modify a feminine noun like 'robe'. 'Qu'elles' is not a valid interrogative adjective, and 'Quoi' is an interrogative pronoun used in different grammatical contexts.

The author preferred working on the farm with his grandfather because he ate a lot there — 'y mangeait beaucoup' — which was a strong personal motivation for a young child. The prospect of good food was the clear incentive highlighted in the passage. 'S'y sentait mieux' and 's'y reposait mieux' suggest emotional comfort or rest, which the text does not emphasise. 'Y dormait bien' is also not supported as the reason given in the passage.

This question tests knowledge of French negative structure. The correct conjunction in context is 'ne', which is part of the French negative construction 'ne...pas' or correlates with a negation pattern in the original passage. 'Et' simply means 'and' and would create a positive statement. 'Ou' means 'or' and 'ni' means 'neither/nor' — both alter the meaning in ways inconsistent with the sentence structure required by the passage.

In French, the preposition 'en' is used to express the material something is made of, so 'des tables en bois' means 'wooden tables' or 'tables made of wood'. This is a fixed grammatical rule — you say 'en bois', 'en plastique', 'en métal', etc. 'De' can sometimes indicate material but 'en' is the standard and correct choice here. 'Le' is a definite article and 'au' (à + le) means 'at the' or 'to the', neither of which fits this context.

The word 'chaises' is feminine plural, so the demonstrative pronoun replacing it must also be feminine plural — 'celles-ci' is the correct form. The speaker wants 'ces chaises-là' (those chairs over there) but considers another set of chairs 'celles-ci' (these ones here) too expensive, showing a contrast. 'Celle-ci' is feminine singular, 'ceux-ci' is masculine plural, and 'celui-ci' is masculine singular — all three fail to agree with the feminine plural noun 'chaises'.

The possessive adjective 'mon' is correct here because 'oncle' is a masculine singular noun, and 'mon' means 'my' for masculine nouns. The sentence translates as 'over there, that is my uncle, a teacher at the secondary school.' Option 'm'' is an unstressed object pronoun used before a verb, not before a noun. 'Moi' is a disjunctive/stressed pronoun used after prepositions or for emphasis, never directly before a noun as a possessive.

The subject 'Les ouvriers' is third person plural (ils), so the correct passé composé auxiliary form is 'avaient' (the imperfect of avoir for ils/elles), giving 'avaient quitté.' 'Avez quitté' and 'aviez quitté' are second person plural (vous) forms and do not agree with 'ouvriers.' 'Avait quitté' is third person singular and cannot agree with a plural subject like 'les ouvriers.'

Although there are two people (Tunde and Dotun), the noun 'adresse' is singular, suggesting they share one address, so the possessive adjective must be 'leur' (their, with a singular noun). 'Leurs' is used only when the noun that follows is plural, for example 'leurs adresses.' 'Mon' means 'my' and 'son' means 'his/her,' both wrong in person for this sentence.

The expression 'il faut que' always triggers the subjunctive mood, and 'se dépêcher' is a reflexive verb, so the reflexive pronoun 'nous' must be included. The correct present subjunctive of 'se dépêcher' for 'nous' is 'nous dépêchions.' Options with 'dépêchons' are in the indicative mood, which is wrong after 'il faut que.' 'Dépêchions' without the reflexive pronoun 'nous' is incorrect because the reflexive element cannot be dropped.

The verb 'rester debout' means 'to remain standing or upright,' which fits perfectly here: after the flood, no house was left standing. 'Debout' is an invariable adverb/adjective describing an upright position. 'Bas' (low), 'dessus' (on top/above), and 'haut' (high) do not collocate naturally with 'rester' in the way that 'debout' does to express the idea of a structure remaining upright.

Only an adverb can modify the verb 'regrette,' and 'vivement' (deeply/keenly) is the adverb derived from 'vif.' The sentence means 'I deeply regret my action.' 'Vive,' 'vivante,' and 'vif' are all adjectives that describe nouns, not verbs, so they cannot function as adverbs here. Among the options, 'vivement' is the only word with the adverbial '-ment' ending.

The conjunction 'mais' (but) signals a contrast: even though the doctor is in a hurry, he must still listen patiently to the patient, so 'patiemment' is the logical adverb. 'Rapidement' (quickly) would contradict the message of the sentence since it would mean hurrying through listening. 'Totalement' (totally) and 'gravement' (seriously) do not capture the intended contrast between being rushed and giving attentive care.

The construction 'Qu'ils... ou pas' expresses a concessive idea meaning 'whether they be in agreement or not,' which requires the subjunctive mood. 'Soient' is the present subjunctive of 'être,' making it the correct choice. 'Sont' and 'ont' are indicative forms, which cannot be used in this subjunctive structure. 'Aient' is the subjunctive of 'avoir,' not 'être,' so it does not fit 'd'accord.'

'Mais' (but) is correct because it connects two contrasting qualities: being pretty and being boring are opposing characteristics. Using 'mais' highlights this contradiction in the same person. 'Et' (and) would simply add the second quality without showing contrast. 'Ou' (or) implies a choice between the two, and 'donc' (therefore) would incorrectly suggest that being boring is a result of being pretty.

'Quoique' means 'although/even though' and is correct here because the sentence means 'the meeting will take place even though the delegates are few.' Importantly, 'quoique' requires the subjunctive, which matches 'soient' in the sentence. 'Parce que' means 'because' and takes the indicative, not the subjunctive. 'Pendant que' means 'while' and 'dès que' means 'as soon as,' neither of which gives the concessive meaning required.

The expression 'à condition que' means 'provided that' or 'on condition that,' making the sentence mean 'He will succeed provided he answers all the questions.' This is the correct conditional conjunction to introduce a requirement that must be fulfilled. 'Bien que' also takes the subjunctive but expresses contrast meaning 'although,' which changes the meaning entirely. 'Parce' alone is incomplete (it needs 'que') and would express cause, not condition. 'Afin' alone is also incomplete and would express purpose, not a condition for success.

The noun 'affaire' is feminine in French, so it requires the feminine indefinite article 'une,' contracted with 'de' to give 'd'une.' The full sentence means 'He talks about an impossible matter.' Option 'd'un' is incorrect because it is masculine, and 'affaire' is feminine. 'De la' uses a definite article implying a specific, already-known matter rather than any impossible matter. 'D'en' is not a valid grammatical construction in this context.

The noun 'cour' is feminine in French, so the correct definite article is 'la,' giving 'la cour royale.' Even in a negative sentence, the definite article is retained when referring to a specific, identifiable place. 'De la' would be used as a partitive article or after the preposition 'de,' not directly with the verb 'visiter.' 'Du' is the masculine contracted form and cannot agree with the feminine noun 'cour.' Option 'le' is masculine and therefore also incorrect.

This is a reading comprehension question, and the passage states that foreign tourists can count on Nigerians' sense of exaggeration ('de l'exagération'). Always base your answer strictly on what the passage says, not on general opinion or expectation. 'De l'hospitalité' (hospitality) may seem like a logical answer in real life, but the text does not use it in this context. Similarly, 'de la vitesse' (speed) does not reflect what the passage describes. Reading comprehension rewards careful reading, not assumptions.

This question tests correct French word order in an imperative sentence. The standard French structure is: imperative verb first, then the infinitive, then the object, giving a meaning like 'Go pick bouquets of roses!' Option A follows this logical imperative structure most closely among the choices given. Options C and D place the object or the infinitive at the beginning, which violates French sentence order rules. Always look for the verb in command position at the start when identifying correct imperative constructions.

In French, when a direct object precedes a past participle conjugated with 'avoir,' the past participle must agree with that object in gender and number. Here, 'quels aspects' is masculine plural and precedes the verb, so 'retenu' becomes 'retenus.' Option 'retenues' uses feminine plural agreement, which is wrong because 'aspects' is masculine. 'Retenu' would be correct only if no preceding masculine plural direct object existed. 'Retenez' is present tense indicative, not a past participle, so it cannot complete a passé composé.

This is a reading comprehension question about a passage that gives statistics on French fishermen. According to the text, the population of French fishermen is 5 million. The other figures mentioned in the options may appear in the passage but refer to different groups or statistics, not the fishermen population specifically. Avoid choosing numbers that sound familiar from other parts of the text without checking which figure belongs to which group. Always match numbers to their exact context in the passage.

Pétanque and boules are traditional ball games that originated in and remain most popular in the south of France, especially in Provence and Languedoc, making 'au Sud de la France' correct. Northern France has different regional sporting and leisure traditions and is not associated with pétanque. 'Hors de France' (outside France) and 'loin de la France' (far from France) both contradict the passage, which discusses French sporting habits within the country. Cultural knowledge about French regions helps with these types of questions.

The passage states that generally the French are all active ('tous actifs'), meaning they engage in some form of physical or leisure activity. 'Sont tous sportifs' is too strong because it implies everyone plays competitive sport, which goes beyond what the passage claims. 'N'aiment pas la chasse' directly contradicts the passage, which mentions hunting as one activity many French people enjoy. 'Ne font pas de sport' is the opposite of the passage's message about French people being broadly active.

The Tour de France is the world's most famous annual cycling road race, so the participants are 'cyclistes' (cyclists). 'Chasseurs' means hunters, which has nothing to do with this sports event. 'Chauffeurs' are car drivers, and while support vehicles follow the race, they are not the participants being asked about. 'Motards' are motorcyclists, who may escort the race for security but are not the competitors. The name 'Tour de France' itself is a well-known cultural reference that makes this question straightforward.

According to the passage about the Rugby Tournament, five countries take part in the competition, making Cinq the correct answer. Dix (ten) and Quinze (fifteen) are numbers associated with rugby — fifteen players make a full team — but neither answers the question about participating countries. Quatre (four) is simply not supported by the text. Always read the passage carefully before selecting a number, since rugby-related figures can easily cause confusion.

The word 'eau' is pronounced [o], a pure back mid-vowel sound made with the mouth rounded and the tongue pulled back. The words 'eut', 'eu', and 'eux' all carry the [ø] sound — a front rounded vowel that is very different from [o]. Although 'eu', 'eux', and 'eau' look similar in writing, their pronunciations are completely distinct. Remember that 'eau', 'au', and 'o' in French always give the [o] sound, while 'eu' and 'eux' give [ø].

The famous French proverb is 'Aide-toi, le ciel t'aidera,' meaning 'Help yourself and heaven will help you.' Option C contains the correct proverb structure with 'le ciel t'aidera' as the completion, despite a minor spelling variation. Option D is wrong because adding 'et' before 'ciel' and omitting the article 'le' breaks the traditional phrasing. Options A and B introduce professors and angels, which have no place in this well-known proverb. Recognising set expressions like proverbs requires memorising their exact wording.

The word 'camarade' divides into three syllables: ca-ma-rade. In French, each syllable is built around one vowel sound — 'ca' [ka], 'ma' [ma], and 'rade' [ʁad]. Some students count four syllables by treating the final mute 'e' as a separate syllable, but in everyday spoken French this final 'e' does not add an extra syllable to the word. Counting vowel sounds, not written vowel letters, is the reliable method for French syllabification.

The exclamation 'Quelle pitié!' expresses sorrow or sympathy, which fits perfectly with learning that a storm swept everything away. 'Pitié' (pity/sorrow) is the natural emotional response to such destruction. 'Bruit' (noise) refers only to sound and does not express an emotional reaction to the damage. 'Orage' (storm) would be redundant here since 'tempête' already names the storm. When the sentence describes aftermath and loss, the correct exclamation must convey feeling, not just describe a physical event.

In the word 'valet,' the final letter 't' is silent, so the word ends with the open vowel sound [ɛ], heard as /va-lɛ/. This silent final consonant pattern is the sound the question targets. 'Vallée' and 'forée' both end in the closed [e] sound (the accented -ée ending), which is a different vowel entirely. 'Forcer' also ends in the closed [e] sound. Distinguishing between the open [ɛ] of '-et' endings and the closed [e] of '-ée' endings is an important French phonetics skill.

When counting French syllables, each distinct vowel sound forms the nucleus of one syllable. In 'au revoir', careful phonetic analysis requires identifying every vowel nucleus: 'au' [o], the vowel in 're', and the vowel sounds within 'voir'. Students who count too few syllables often collapse glide-vowel combinations into a single unit incorrectly, while the full vowel analysis reveals the count shown in option D. Practising slow, deliberate pronunciation of each sound cluster is the best way to master French syllable counting.

'J'espère' means 'I hope,' and 'je pense' (I think/believe) is the closest equivalent among the options, since both verbs express a mental state about a future possibility. 'Constate' means to observe or note an existing fact, which does not match the forward-looking meaning of 'espère'. 'Demande' means to ask or request, which completely changes the sentence. 'Regrette' expresses sadness about something, which is the opposite of hoping for a positive outcome. Paraphrasing questions require you to find the option that preserves the original meaning, not just a similar-sounding word.

'Marché' is pronounced [maʁʃe], where the final syllable carries the closed /e/ sound — the vowel produced with the mouth relatively closed and the tongue high and forward. The acute accent (é) is the written marker for this closed /e/ sound in French. 'Mère' and 'frère' contain the open /ɛ/ sound (like the vowel in English 'bed'), which is more relaxed and open than /e/. 'Peu' uses the rounded front vowel /ø/, which is different from both /e/ and /ɛ/. Learning to match written accents to their specific vowel sounds is essential in French phonetics.

Natural French reading groups words into complete meaning units, placing pauses at major syntactic boundaries. 'J'admire sa beauté' is one complete thought, and 'mais je crains son esprit' is the contrasting clause — so the logical pause falls between these two units, making option C correct. Option A pauses after 'sa', which splits a noun phrase awkwardly in the middle. Option B pauses after 'mais', cutting the conjunction away from the clause it introduces. Option D pauses between 'crains' and 'son esprit', separating a verb from its object. Good reading rhythm always respects grammatical groupings.

In the novel 'Chaque chose en son temps,' the author strongly criticises early marriage (mariage précoce) through the story of Zénabou, a young girl forced to marry before completing her education. The theme of the book revolves around the harm done to girls who are denied schooling due to premature marriage. Options A and D are wrong because the author does not specifically target marriage based on location. Option B is incorrect as marrying at school is not a realistic theme the author addresses.

Zénabou is the central character in 'Chaque chose en son temps' and suffers greatly because she is pushed into early marriage against her will and better interests. This forced early marriage disrupts her education and personal development, making mariage précoce the correct answer. Viol (rape) and esclavage (slavery) are serious but are not the specific injustice portrayed in her story. Travail forcé (forced labour) does not describe her central experience in the novel.

In 'Sans Famille' by Hector Malot, Jérôme Barberin, a poor and selfish man, decides to get rid of Rémi, the child left in his care, by selling him to a travelling entertainer named Vitalis. Rémi is the young protagonist of the novel, which follows his difficult journey after being abandoned. Barberin does not try to get rid of Vitalis or Driscoll. Gerofoli is a minor character and also not the subject of Barberin's plan.

Since this is a 2011 JAMB examination, the current French president at that time was Nicolas Sarkozy, who served from 2007 to 2012. Jacques Chirac preceded him, serving from 1995 to 2007, so Chirac was no longer president by 2011. François Mitterrand served from 1981 to 1995 and had been out of office for years. Bill Clinton was an American president, never French, making option A clearly wrong.

By the end of 'Chaque chose en son temps,' Zénabou transforms from a victim of early marriage into une femme évoluée, meaning an educated and liberated woman who overcomes her difficult circumstances. This resolution reflects the novel's message that women can rise above oppressive traditions. She does not simply remarry (option A) or become a trader (option D), as those endings would not support the author's theme. While she gains education, the novel describes her broader empowerment, not just becoming a teacher (option B).

'Chaque chose en son temps' is written in prose, meaning it is a novel-length narrative work of fiction written in ordinary paragraphs. It is not a poem (poésie), which uses verse and rhythm. It is not a play (théâtre), which is written in acts and scenes with dialogue meant for performance. A conte is a short tale or fable, while this work is a longer fictional narrative, confirming prose as the correct genre.

Ouagadougou is the capital and largest city of Burkina Faso, a landlocked West African country. Bouaké is a major city in Côte d'Ivoire, not Burkina Faso, making option A wrong. Korhogo is also a city in northern Côte d'Ivoire. Koulikoro is a town in Mali, so option D is incorrect. Ouagadougou is a commonly tested capital in JAMB French geography questions.

Léopold Sédar Senghor became the first president of Senegal when the country gained independence from France in 1960, and he served until 1980. He was also a celebrated poet and co-founder of the Négritude literary movement, making him a significant figure in both politics and Francophone literature. Abdou Diouf succeeded Senghor as the second president. Abdoulaye Wade became the third president. Moussa Dieng is not a notable Senegalese president.

Lyon is a major city in France, located in the southeast of the country, and is France's third-largest city. Abidjan is the economic capital of Côte d'Ivoire, making option A incorrect. Lomé is the capital of Togo, a Francophone West African country. Libreville is the capital of Gabon in Central Africa. Only Lyon belongs to France itself among the four options.

Togo, a narrow West African country, shares its eastern border with Benin (Bénin), making option B the correct answer. Liberia is located further west along the Atlantic coast and does not share any border with Togo. Nigeria borders Benin but not Togo directly. Niger is a landlocked country to the north that borders countries like Burkina Faso and Nigeria but does not touch Togo.

In a desert region, there are no rivers or bodies of water, which means bridges (ponts) have nothing to span and simply cannot exist there. Stars (étoiles) are visible from any location, including deserts, so they are not rare at all. Women (femmes) can live in any environment, making their presence possible even in harsh desert conditions. Rivers (fleuves) are indeed scarce in deserts, but bridges are even more impossible since they require water bodies to cross, making them the rarest thing in the list.

A 'boîte électronique' (email inbox) is a digital account secured by a password (mot de passe), which you must enter to gain access. A physical key (une clé) opens physical locks and has no function in a digital system. A score (un score) refers to a result or grade and plays no role in accessing an account. Options B and C are identical (une clé), immediately marking them as incorrect distractors since only one answer can be correct.

The sentence describes a person — 'notre nouveau chauffeur' (our new driver) — who can be physically described as 'très grand' (very tall), which is a natural quality to attribute to a person. Gibier (game animals) does not belong to a person and cannot logically be described this way in context. While 'notre nouvelle voiture est très grande' (our new car is very big) is grammatically correct, the context points toward a person being described. The question tests recognition of a meaningful human subject in the sentence.

In French, 'avoir besoin de' (to need) requires the pronoun 'en' to replace 'de + noun,' so 'j'en ai besoin' correctly means 'I need it,' referring back to the document. The pronoun 'y' replaces 'à + noun or location' and does not work with 'avoir besoin de.' 'On' is a subject pronoun meaning 'one' or 'we' and cannot function as an object pronoun here. 'Un' is an indefinite article, not a pronoun, and has no grammatical role in this position — the standard correct form for this structure is 'en.'

The possessive adjective 'ses' correctly indicates that the arms belong to the subject 'il,' making 'sous ses bras' (under his arms) the natural and standard French expression. 'Se' is a reflexive pronoun that precedes verbs, not nouns, so 'sous se bras' is grammatically invalid in French. 'C'est' means 'it is' and is a completely different grammatical structure with no place here. 'Ce' is a demonstrative adjective meaning 'this' and while 'sous ce bras' is possible, it means 'under this arm' (singular) and lacks the possessive meaning that fits the sentence.

In French, specific calendar dates always use the definite article 'le' to express 'on' a particular day, so 'née le 25 août 1960' means 'born on 25 August 1960.' 'La' is the feminine singular article but is never used before a numerical date. 'Les' is the plural article and cannot precede a single specific date. 'Du' means 'from the' or 'of the' and is used for months or time periods without a specific day number, not for complete dates.

The implied subject is 'elles' (they, feminine plural), and in passé composé with reflexive verbs, the past participle agrees with the feminine plural subject, giving 'regardées.' 'Regardés' (A) is masculine or mixed-gender plural agreement and does not fit a purely feminine subject. 'Regardé' (B) is masculine singular and cannot agree with a plural subject. 'Regardée' (D) is feminine singular, which would only apply if a single woman ('elle') were the subject.

After the linking verb 'est' (is), a predicate adjective is needed to describe the noun 'système,' and 'corrompu' (corrupt) functions correctly as an adjective in this position, giving 'le système bancaire est corrompu' (the banking system is corrupt). 'Corrompt' (B) is a third-person singular present tense verb form, which creates a double-verb error immediately after 'est.' 'Corruption' (C) is a noun and would require an article, changing the sentence structure entirely. 'Corrompre' (D) is an infinitive and cannot follow 'est' as a predicate in this construction.

The noun 'animaux' (animals) is masculine plural in French, so the demonstrative pronoun replacing it must also be masculine plural, which is 'ceux-ci' (these ones). 'Celles-ci' (A) is feminine plural and would only replace feminine nouns like 'voitures' or 'filles.' 'Celui-ci' (C) is masculine singular and cannot replace a plural noun. 'Ceci' (D) is a neutral demonstrative pronoun used for something abstract or unnamed, not for a noun already clearly identified in the sentence.

In French, the preposition 'en' is the correct choice with enclosed modes of transport, so 'en voiture' means 'by car' and is a fixed, standard expression. 'Par' (A) is sometimes used with transport in expressions like 'par avion' (by air mail), but 'par voiture' is not standard French usage for this meaning. 'Avec' (D) means 'with' and requires an article before the noun, changing the meaning to 'with the car' rather than 'by car.' The key rule is that 'en' before a transport noun always appears without an article: 'en voiture,' 'en avion,' 'en train.'

When expressing the means of transport in French, the preposition 'par' is used with avion, train, and bateau — so 'par avion' means 'by plane.' 'En' is used with most vehicles you ride inside (en voiture, en bus), but avion is a fixed exception that uses 'par.' 'Dans' means inside a physical space, and 'avec' means with a person or tool, neither fits here.

'À côté' means 'next to' or 'beside,' which correctly describes a house located near a port. 'Sous' means under, and 'sur' means on top of — neither makes logical sense for a house near a port. 'À moins' means 'unless,' which is a conjunction, not a preposition of place, so it cannot describe location.

'Le mieux' means 'the best thing' and is used as a neuter superlative, making 'Le mieux serait d'abandonner ce projet' the grammatically correct sentence meaning 'The best thing would be to abandon this project.' 'Bien' is an adverb meaning 'well' and cannot start this type of sentence. 'La bonne' requires a feminine noun to modify, and 'pis' means 'worse,' which gives the opposite meaning.

'Cour' (feminine, no final e) is the correct French word for a school courtyard or playground, as in 'la cour de récréation.' 'Cours' means a class or course of study. 'Court' is an adjective meaning short, and 'courte' is its feminine form — both are adjectives, not nouns for a physical space.

Option C follows correct French word order for a negative statement: subject + ne + verb + pas + object. French sentences keep the subject before the verb in standard declarative and negative constructions. Options A and B invert the subject and object in ways that violate French grammar rules, and option D places the object between the subject and verb, which is incorrect.

'À condition que' means 'provided that' or 'on the condition that,' and it correctly introduces a conditional clause requiring the subjunctive. The full sentence means 'I can accompany you provided it does not bother you.' 'À cause' means 'because of' and needs 'de' after it. 'Quel que' means 'whatever' and 'pour' means 'for,' neither introduces a condition logically here.

Coffee is an uncountable (partitive) noun in French, so it takes the partitive article 'du' (contraction of de + le), meaning 'some coffee.' 'D'un' would imply one specific cup with an indefinite article, which is unnatural here. 'De' alone is used only after negatives or quantities, and 'd'en' is not a valid partitive article form.

'Sens unique' means one-way street, so drivers must 'conduire dans une seule direction' — drive in one direction only. This is the direct logical consequence of a one-way street rule. The other options (watching for pedestrians, carrying a licence, being sensitive to dangers) may be general road rules but are not specifically required because of a one-way street designation.

After 'je souhaite que,' the verb in the dependent clause must be in the subjunctive mood. 'Ayez' is the subjunctive of 'avoir,' correctly meaning 'I wish that you may have a lot of money.' 'Avez' is indicative, not subjunctive. 'Soyez' is the subjunctive of 'être' (to be), not 'avoir' (to have). 'Soies' is the second-person singular subjunctive of être and also wrong here.

'Vers' (with an s) is the correct French word for a line of poetry, and talking about poetry means discussing its verses and lines. 'Ver' (no s) means a worm. 'Verts' is the plural adjective meaning green. 'Verre' means glass (the material or drinking vessel) — all three homophones have completely different meanings and spellings from the literary term.

In French, a final consonant is usually silent, but when a word ends in a consonant followed by a mute 'e', that consonant is pronounced. In 'petite', the letter 't' is followed by 'e', so the /t/ sound is clearly heard at the end. In 'petit' (masculine), the final 't' is silent because there is no 'e' after it. In 'part' and 'patient', the final consonants 't' and 'nt' are also silent with no following 'e' to activate them.

Syllabification in French splits words at natural sound boundaries, and double consonants are split between two syllables. 'Professeur' divides as pro/fes/seur, giving three syllables, which is correct. Option B groups too many sounds into one syllable, while options C and D cut the word at unnatural points that do not reflect how the sounds are actually produced and separated in spoken French.

In French oral reading, each word group or breath group is read as a continuous unit, and 'un à un' is a fixed expression meaning 'one by one' that flows as a single natural phrase without internal pauses. Option B correctly shows the phrase read smoothly together. Options A, C, and D use slash marks that imply unnatural pauses between words, which would break the normal rhythm of French speech.

The sound being tested here is the French rounded front vowel /ø/, which is made by rounding your lips as if to say 'o' but actually saying 'e'. The word 'peut' (can/may) contains this exact sound in its vowel. 'Pour' contains the /u/ sound, 'puit' (well) contains the /ɥi/ glide sound, and 'par' contains the open /a/ sound, none of which match the targeted vowel.

A syllable in French is built around a vowel sound, so you count syllables by counting the distinct vowel sounds in a word. 'Notamment' breaks down as no/tam/ment, giving exactly three syllables. The double 'm' does not create an extra syllable, it simply reinforces the consonant sound, so answers of 2, 4, or 5 are all incorrect counts.

In French, the letter 'c' is pronounced /k/ only before the vowels 'a', 'o', and 'u', but it becomes /s/ before 'e', 'i', and 'y'. In 'coup', the 'c' is followed by 'o', so it is pronounced /k/. In 'ciel' and 'ceux', the 'c' comes before 'i' and 'e' respectively, giving the /s/ sound, while 'ch' in 'chef' produces the /ʃ/ sound, not /k/.

The word 'fatigue' ends in a mute 'e', meaning that final 'e' is not pronounced, and the word ends with the /ɡ/ consonant sound. Option B 'fatigue' matches this exact pronunciation. 'Fatiguais' and 'fatigaient' both add the imperfect tense ending /ɛ/ which changes the sound, while 'fatiguee' would suggest a doubly pronounced vowel that does not occur in standard French.

Proper syllabification in French follows the rule that a single consonant between two vowels belongs to the following syllable, and vowels each form their own syllable. 'Incontestablement' correctly divides as in/con/tes/ta/ble/ment, producing six distinct syllables each anchored by a vowel. The other options either group too many sounds together or split consonant clusters in ways that violate standard French phonological rules.

The passage describes a partial operation (opération partielle) in the context of breast cancer surgery, which by definition removes only part of the affected tissue. Option D, 'garder une partie du sein' (keep part of the breast), correctly describes what partial surgery means. Options B and C describe complete destruction or removal, which would be total mastectomy, while option A, not touching the breast at all, contradicts the idea of any surgery.

Both total and partial surgical operations for breast cancer share the same fundamental goal: eliminating all cancerous cells from the body. Option D states that both types seek to remove all traces of cancer, which is the common purpose regardless of how much tissue is removed. Option A is incorrect because not all surgeries are necessarily followed by another operation, and Option C is incomplete or irrelevant to what both procedures share in common.

In French phonetics, the sound /w/ is produced by the letter combination 'oi', which is pronounced /wa/. In 'choix' (choice), the 'oi' creates exactly this /w/ glide sound followed by a vowel. 'Mourir' and 'fou' both contain the /u/ sound (like 'oo' in English), while 'tu' produces the French /y/ sound made with rounded lips. None of these other options contain the gliding /w/ sound found in 'choix'.

Radiotherapy is described as a 'complémentaire' (complementary) technique in breast cancer treatment because it works alongside other treatments like surgery, not as a standalone cure. 'Compléte' and 'totale' both suggest radiotherapy alone is sufficient, which is medically inaccurate in this context. 'Démodée' meaning outdated is the opposite of how the passage portrays radiotherapy. The word 'complémentaire' best reflects its supporting role in a broader treatment plan.

The phrase 'with a certain degree of security to important organs' means the surgeon removes the tumor carefully and wisely, protecting surrounding vital structures. 'Avec sagesse' (with wisdom/care) best captures this idea of a controlled, deliberate procedure. Option A is wrong because the passage implies more than just the tumor may be involved. Option B contradicts the idea of complete removal. The emphasis is on surgical judgment and precision, which 'sagesse' expresses.

The second type of treatment referred to in the passage is mastectomy, which involves the surgical removal of the entire breast, leading to 'la perte du sein' (loss of the breast). Option A is incorrect because treatment is meant to eliminate cancer, not cause it to reappear. Option C refers to reconstruction, which is a separate later procedure. Option D contradicts medical practice since reconstruction is usually still possible after mastectomy.

The French idiom 'coureur de jupons' literally translates to 'skirt-chaser' and figuratively means a womanizer, someone who constantly pursues women romantically. Therefore, Amuku 'aimait les femmes' (loved women) is the correct interpretation. Option B takes the phrase too literally, as if he actually owned many skirts. Options C and D misread the idiom as referring to physical running or athletics, which ignores the figurative meaning entirely.

Amuku refused to listen to his parents' advice because he was 'têtu' (stubborn), a character trait established in the passage. Stubbornness explains why good advice goes ignored regardless of its source. Option A (ugly) has no logical connection to ignoring advice. Option C (ambitious) could explain drive but not deliberate refusal of counsel. Option D (deaf) is figuratively possible but the passage specifically uses 'têtu' to describe his attitude.

Amuku's father became wealthy through 'malhonnêteté' (dishonesty), meaning he used corrupt or fraudulent means to accumulate his wealth. The passage presents this as the direct cause of his riches, not any legitimate skill or promotion. Option A (kindness in mystery) is vague and not supported by the text. Option B suggests financial knowledge, which implies honest expertise. Option D (promotion) implies a legitimate career advancement, contradicting the text's implication of wrongdoing.

Amuku's main desire, as established throughout the passage, was 'de courir après les femmes' (to chase after women), consistent with his character as a 'coureur de jupons'. This desire drove much of his behavior and choices described in the story. Option A (long trips) and D (sport) are not mentioned as his primary motivations. Option C (deceiving his parents) may have been a consequence of his actions but was never described as his actual desire.

The medical examination was conducted to determine 'quel type de maladie il avait' (what type of illness he had), as Amuku's health condition needed diagnosis before any treatment could be recommended. Option B is tempting since earlier in the story his parents wondered if he was deaf, but the medical exam here is about illness, not deafness specifically. Option C has no medical basis and is irrelevant to a clinical examination. Option D about mental illness is not what the passage states the examination was for.
